explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Verse 2 puts the Spirit of God right there over the dark water, before any light shows up. Nobody else is named in the scene. Before the first word is even spoken, God is already on the job.

I see why an angel came to mind. But no angel is mentioned anywhere in these verses. The text says it is “…the Spirit of God…” hovering over the surface of the waters. Sometimes the answer is the one sitting right there on the page.
The cherubim never show up in this passage. Verse 2 names “…the Spirit of God…” hovering over the surface of the waters. Cherubim sounds so grand that I almost wanted it to be right, friend.

Yes, friend! In verse 3, God said, “Let there be light…” and there was light. He said it, and there it was. It's the first time God speaks in the story, and I think that's a pretty strong way to start talking.

Fire is a good guess, and I'll admit I'm partial to anything hot. But in verse 3 the thing God calls into being is light. No fire is mentioned in these verses. A first day with fire would have been a whole different story, friend.
Thunder would make for a dramatic opening, like a drum roll. But the text skips the drum roll. God says, “Let there be light…” and there was light (verse 3). No thunder in these verses, friend.

Verse 4 says God “…separated the light from the darkness.” Then in verse 5 He gives each one a name, “day” and “night.” Naming something is a big deal, friend. I labeled cookie boxes for years and never felt that official.
The text says God separated the light from the darkness (verse 4). Nothing in these verses says He blended them. Then in verse 5 each gets its own name, “day” and “night.”

The darkness doesn't go anywhere. God separated the light from the darkness, and then in verse 5 He called the darkness “night.” So the darkness stays, with a name of its own. Nobody got kicked out of this story, friend.

Verse 5 says, “God called the light ‘day,’ and the darkness He called ‘night.’” So God does the naming Himself, and day and night get their names right there. It's a simple pair, and I appreciate that. Some folks need three tries to name a pet goldfish.

Shadow sounds like a superhero who only works at dusk. But God's word for the darkness in verse 5 is “night.” Shadow is a nice word, just not the one the text uses. Next time, I'll be listening for “night.”

Gloom sounds like how I feel when my timer goes off and the batch is already dark. But in verse 5 God calls the darkness “night.” That's the name the text gives. Gloom doesn't show up anywhere in this passage.

Verse 7 says God made the expanse and “…separated the waters beneath it from the waters above.” So there are waters on both sides of it. Some below, some above, and the expanse sits in the middle. In verse 8 He calls it “sky.”

This one is actually true, friend. The text says God made the expanse and “…separated the waters beneath it from the waters above.” So some waters are beneath it and some are above it. In verse 8 He calls the expanse “sky.”
Verse 8 says, “God called the expanse ‘sky.’” That's the name He gives the space between the waters. And that wraps up the second day. Nice and short, friend, the way I like my names.

A valley is something that sits on the land, and the land hasn't even appeared yet on day two. The expanse sits between the waters, and verse 8 says God called it “sky.” No valley in these verses. Good thing I'm not in charge of maps.
Rivers don't come up anywhere in this passage. What God names in verse 8 is the expanse between the waters, and He calls it “sky.” It's a high-up name, friend, for a high-up thing.

explanations.answer: So the dry land may appear
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what verse 9 says. God says, “Let the waters under the sky be gathered into one place, so that the dry land may appear.” The waters gather, and the dry land shows up. Then in verse 10 He calls the dry land “earth.”

explanations.answer: So the waters can grow deeper
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason. In verse 9, God says the waters should be gathered into one place “…so that the dry land may appear.” Deeper water isn't mentioned at all. The goal is dry land, friend.

explanations.answer: So the light can shine on them
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, friend, but light already showed up back in verse 3. The reason God gives in verse 9 is “…so that the dry land may appear.” The waters aren't gathering to be lit up. They're making room, like clearing boxes off a counter so there's space to work.

Close, friend, but that's not what verse 11 says. God says, “Let the earth bring forth vegetation…” So the plants come from the earth, and the seas aren't part of it. The dry land showed up just before this.
That's right. In verse 11, God says, “Let the earth bring forth vegetation…” So He tells the earth to bring forth the plants, not the seas. And verse 12 says the earth produced them.
Seed is the word, friend. Verse 11 says each tree bears “…fruit with seed according to its kind.” Chocolate chips belong in my cookies, but in this verse the seed belongs in the fruit.
Honey would make a sweet fruit tree, I'll give you that. But the text says each tree bears fruit with seed in it. Honey doesn't appear anywhere in verse 11.
Oil isn't in this verse, friend. Verse 11 says the trees bear “…fruit with seed according to its kind.” The seed is the thing inside the fruit. You can set the oil aside for another passage.

explanations.answer: Mark the seasons and days and years
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Verse 14 says, “…and let them be signs to mark the seasons and days and years.” So the lights in the sky are also signs for keeping track of time. Seasons, days, years, all of it. Somebody should tell my timer it has competition.

explanations.answer: Warn of the storms coming in
explanations.explanation: Storms don't come up in these verses at all, friend. What verse 14 says is that the lights are to “…mark the seasons and days and years.” That's their job here. A weather warning isn't on the list.

explanations.answer: Guide the sailors across the sea
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a handy job for a light in the sky. But the passage doesn't mention sailors or ships. Verse 14 says the lights are to “…mark the seasons and days and years.” That's what the text gives them.
Verse 16 says, “God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night.” So the greater light is the one over the day. Big light, big daytime job, friend.
You've got the other light there, friend. In verse 16, it's the lesser light that is made to rule the night. The greater light rules the day. They split the shifts.

The seas aren't ruled by either light in this verse. Verse 16 says the greater light rules the day, and the lesser light rules the night. The seas get their own mention elsewhere in the passage. These two have the day and the night.

There's one more thing, friend. Verse 16 ends with “And He made the stars as well.” So the two great lights aren't the only ones God made for the sky on day four. The stars are right there, tucked in at the end.

That's right. Verse 16 says God made the two great lights, and then adds, “And He made the stars as well.” So the sky gets stars on day four, too. It's a short line, so it's easy to blink and miss it.

Yes, friend. Verse 16 says God made “the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night.” So the lesser light is the one over the night. And the verse adds one more thing: “And He made the stars as well.”

That one is actually true. Verse 16 says God made “the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night.” So the lesser light is the one over the night. It's easy to flip the two when they're in the same sentence.

Verse 20 says, “Let the waters teem with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth in the open expanse of the sky.” So the birds get the sky, and the waters get the teeming creatures. Everybody gets a place to be, friend.
Angels aren't in these verses. In verse 20, it's birds that God says will fly above the earth in the open expanse of the sky. Flying creatures, yes, but these are the feathered kind.

Locusts aren't in this passage, friend, and I'm glad. A swarm of anything in a bakery is a rough day for a cookie box. Verse 20 says it's birds that fly above the earth in the open expanse of the sky.

That's it. Verse 22 says God blessed them and said, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters of the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.” So the blessing comes with a command to multiply. The sea creatures fill the waters, and the birds multiply on the earth.

Not quite, friend. In verse 22, God blesses them and tells the sea creatures to be fruitful, multiply and fill the waters, and the birds to multiply on the earth. Nothing in the blessing tells them to stay put. I stayed put in a drawer for years, and I can tell you it wasn't my favorite way to spend a decade.

Rest shows up later in the passage, friend, but it's for God on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2). Here in verse 22, the blessing words are “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters of the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.” That's about multiplying, not napping.

Not quite, friend. Verse 24 says, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds…” So the land creatures come from the earth, not from the seas. The sea creatures already had their turn on day five.

That's right. On day six, God says, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds: livestock, land crawlers, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds.” So the call goes to the earth. The seas had their creatures on day five.

That's right, friend. In verse 26, God says man is to “…rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air…” and over the livestock and the earth too. The list goes from the sea to the sky to the ground. That's a lot of territory to be handed, and I get nervous just managing one bakery.

Offerings aren't mentioned in these verses. God says man will “…rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the livestock, and over all the earth itself and every creature that crawls upon it.” Rule is the word in verse 26.
That's not what verse 26 says, friend. God says man is “…to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air…” The word is rule, and keeping away isn't in the verse at all.

Verse 28 says God blessed them and told them, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it…” So the earth is what they're to fill. And they aren't alone in being told to multiply, as God said similar words to the creatures earlier.
The seas are what God told the sea creatures to fill in verse 22. For the man and the woman, verse 28 says, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth…” Different group, different place to fill.
The sky isn't what God says to fill here. In verse 28, He tells the man and the woman to “…fill the earth and subdue it…” The birds have the sky, and these two have the earth.

In verse 29, God says, “Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant on the face of all the earth, and every tree whose fruit contains seed. They will be yours for food.” So plants and fruit are what's on the table. I'll stick with cookies, friend, but I'm sure that was a fine menu.

Fish are in the passage, but not on the food list here. Verse 29 says what God has given them for food: “…every seed-bearing plant…” and “…every tree whose fruit contains seed.” The fish are part of what man is to rule over (verse 26).

The livestock are in this passage, but as part of what man is to rule over (verse 26). When God names the food in verse 29, He says, “…every seed-bearing plant on the face of all the earth, and every tree whose fruit contains seed.” So the food He gives is from plants.

Not quite, friend. In verse 30, God says, “…I have given every green plant for food.” He says it about every beast of the earth, every bird of the air and every creature that crawls upon the earth. So He provides for them, and leaving them to find food on their own doesn't match the verse.

Right, friend. In verse 30 God says, “…I have given every green plant for food.” He says it about every beast of the earth, every bird of the air and every creature that crawls upon the earth, “…everything that has the breath of life in it…” Then the verse ends with “And it was so.”

Verse 31 says, “And God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good.” Earlier in the passage, God saw that things were good. Here He looks upon all that He had made, and the word is “very.” Look at that, friend.
“Still good” would be what I say about a cookie that fell on the floor. Verse 31 says it's “very good,” a step up from the earlier “good.” This time God is looking at everything He made.
“Mostly good” is what I tell myself about a cookie with one burnt side. But verse 31 says, “…indeed, it was very good.” There's no “mostly” anywhere in it, friend.

explanations.answer: He rests from all His work
explanations.explanation: Verse 2 says, “so on that day He rested from all His work.” The work is finished, and on the seventh day He rests. It's the last day of the creation week. Friend, I take that as permission to sit down once in a while.

Naming stars isn't mentioned in this passage, friend. The text says God had finished the work He had been doing, “so on that day He rested from all His work.” (verse 2). The seventh day is a rest day.

explanations.answer: He starts a brand new world
explanations.explanation: No new world here. Genesis 2:1 says the heavens and the earth “…were completed in all their vast array.” and verse 2 says He rested from all His work. So the seventh day is a day of rest, not a day for starting over.

explanations.answer: He blesses it and makes it holy
explanations.explanation: Verse 3 says, “…God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it…” So God does two things with this day, friend. He blesses it and He sanctifies it, which means setting it apart as holy. The verse gives the reason: “…because on that day He rested from all the work of creation that He had accomplished.”

explanations.answer: He makes it longer than the rest
explanations.explanation: Nothing in these verses says the seventh day is longer. What verse 3 says is that “…God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it…” Those are the two things God does with the day. Sorry, friend, no extra hours.

explanations.answer: He gives it a brand new name
explanations.explanation: God does name things earlier, like “day,” “night,” “sky,” “earth” and “seas.” But the seventh day gets no new name in these verses. Verse 3 says, “…God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it…” So it's a blessing, not a naming.
